Field brief · mountain-hazard intelligence · Arunachal Pradesh first

The Data Backbone

The idea, the logic, and what stands on it

As of 10 Oct 2026 The idea: 8 minutes Everything: about 17 Idea first, numbers last
Say this · 30 seconds

We are building the data backbone for mountain-hazard intelligence. The facts needed to see a landslide or a flood coming already exist, but they are scattered across satellites, government portals, river gauges and survey maps, in shapes that do not fit together. Every team that wants to use them spends months lining them up, and then that work is thrown away. We do it once. Every source is collected, checked, laid on one shared map of the state and kept current, with a record of where it came from. Anything can then be built on top. Our landslide forecast and our flood forecast are the first two products, and the second cost a fraction of the first. And because every forecast is written down and checked against what really happened, the backbone gets richer every season.

In one line

From fragmented mountain data to actionable intelligence. It is the pitch deck's own closing line.

The picture to hold

An app is a vehicle. The backbone is the road. We are building the road, and running the first two vehicles on it to prove it carries weight.

Why a backbone

The app is the easy part. Four things are broken underneath it.

They are the same four for every hazard, which is why fixing them once is worth more than any single product.

30 m · 250 m · 11 kmground height · soil · rain

The data exists, but in pieces.

It sits with NASA and the European satellites, GSI, ISRO, the state space centre, the water commission and others. Each has its own format and scale. Rock types come as outlines, rivers as lines. Some sit behind portals that look closed and are not.

Start. Publish. Stop.then the next team starts again

Every project starts from zero.

A landslide study spends months lining this up, publishes one map, and stops. The flood study next door does the same work again. Nothing is reused.

Jan = Augthe same map all year

A map made once goes stale.

The ground barely changes, but rain and rivers change every day. A one-off map cannot tell you about this week.

No scorecardsaid, but never checked

Nobody keeps score.

Forecasts are not written down and checked against what happened. So nothing learns, and nobody can prove a forecast was any good.

The result is what you see everywhere: static maps, one-off studies, pilots that never scale. Our own first forecast taught us this. The model was the small part. Finding, checking and lining up the data was most of the work, and all of it was reusable.

The idea

Do the hard part once, and let everything stand on it

It is a standing system, not a one-off study. This is the whole idea in one picture.

Six rules make it work

Rule 1

One map for everything

The state is cut into 8.2 million squares, each the size of a football field. Every source, whatever its shape, becomes one more column of facts about those squares.

WhyA model needs a table. And two products can never disagree about where a place is.
Rule 2

Keep the original, and write down where it came from

Raw files are never edited. Each carries its source, its terms of use, its link, the date it was fetched and a fingerprint.

WhyAnyone can audit a number. If a source goes offline we lose freshness, not the system.
Rule 3

Check a source before trusting it

Every new source is tested against something independent.

WhyOfficial data can be wrong. The only official flood map of the state put most of its "flooded" ground on steep slopes. One wrong river reading once looked like a 52% flood.
Rule 4

The backbone does not know which hazard it serves

Nothing in it says "landslide" or "flood". A product brings its own question.

WhyThis is what makes the second product cheap, and the third cheaper.
Rule 5

Two shelves

One holds ready-to-use data: the map, the facts, the rain history. The other holds answers: forecasts and risk layers.

WhyDifferent people need different shelves. A road planner may want the base layers. An officer wants the forecast.
Rule 6

Close the loop

Every forecast is written down before the day and graded after it. What really happened comes back in as new data.

WhyMore data makes a forecast fresher. Only knowing what happened makes it better.

How it works

Follow one file through

  1. STEP 1

    Collect

    A script fetches each source: satellite archives, government map servers, river gauges, and a live weather feed every day.

  2. STEP 2

    Keep

    The file is stored untouched, with its record.

  3. STEP 3

    Line up

    It is fitted to the shared map. An outline becomes "which rock am I on". A line becomes "how far to the nearest river, road or fault".

  4. STEP 4

    Describe

    Each square ends up with 34 facts, and each place with 26 years of daily rain.

  5. STEP 5

    Shelve

    That table is shelf one. It is the same for every product.

  6. STEP 6

    Ask

    A product asks its two questions of it: where can this happen, and is something setting it off now?

  7. STEP 7

    Answer

    The result goes on shelf two and onto the screen, place by place, for the next seven days.

  8. STEP 8

    Check

    The forecast is written down, and later graded against what happened.

How it helps a product

A product is a question asked of the backbone

What a product gets for free

  • The shared map and its 34 facts per square
  • 26 years of rain, and live rain for the next 7 days
  • Rivers, catchments, roads, places and search
  • Maps, 3D and the app's frame
  • The honest way of testing, and the forecast log and grader

What it adds itself

  • Its WHERE question
  • Its WHEN question
  • Its own record of what happened
  • Its own screen

Four proofs that this is real, not a slogan

2 filesThe first flood module reused everything and added two files of its own maths.
1 rain fetchOne call to the weather feed serves both products.
1 folder, 1 lineThat is what a new module costs inside the app.
It gives backFlood brought in 32 river gauges, a verified flood record, the forecast log and a denser rain grid. The denser rain now feeds the landslide forecast too.

What else can stand on it

More hazards, more places, more users

More hazards

Anything with the WHERE × WHEN shape fits.

  • Soil erosion, for Assam. Next. The department names five ingredients: rain, soil, slope, plant cover, land use. Four are already in the backbone.
  • Glacial-lake floods
  • Forest fire
  • Earthquake-triggered slides
  • Riverbank erosion, city flooding

More places

The satellite inputs are global, so the same steps run anywhere.

  • A new state needs a switch for the region, its own local records, and its own checking.
  • Assam is the first test. Its map is designed to line up square for square with Arunachal's, so a river crossing the border can be followed across it.
  • Then the rest of the Himalayan belt.

More users of the data itself

Through an open feed. None of this exists yet.

  • Road and infrastructure planners
  • Power and telecom operators with assets on unstable ground
  • Insurers and risk modellers
  • Researchers and agencies who need the lined-up base layers
  • The state's own systems, so a warning shows up where officers already work
  • Other startups building their own products

Why it gets stronger with time

It makes its own ground truth

The loop makes new evidence

Each forecast, once graded, becomes a dated, located example that did not exist before.

New kinds of data land on the same map

Our own sensors, drone surveys, field and citizen reports, old road-closure logs and news records. Each becomes one more column, or one more dated event.

Sensors go where the backbone points

It ranks the ground, so it tells you which slopes and rivers deserve an instrument. Their readings then come back in as data.

What is ours

Most inputs are public. What is ours is the assembly, the upkeep and the checked local history. Code can be copied. Seasons of checked local history cannot.

The two products, as proof

◭

SlideSense

Landslide forecast
Live
  • Its WHERE questionHow weak is this ground? Learned from about 37,000 mapped landslides inside Arunachal.
  • Its WHEN questionIs the rain unusual for this exact place?
  • Where it standsA 7-day outlook for any place and for roads. WHERE picks the right spot about 6 times in 7. It gives a rank, not a percentage. Its forecasts are written down every day since 10 October, and not graded yet: nothing feeds dated landslides in.
◈

FloodSense

Flood forecast · the furthest along
Live
  • Its WHERE questionHow easily does water reach this spot?
  • Its WHEN questionRain here and upstream, plus the river's own level at 32 gauges.
  • Where it standsIt runs by itself every morning and grades itself against the real river. At a gauged river, when it says 20%, about 20% happen. It has not yet been through a live flood: logging began as the monsoon ended.

Honest limits

  • Wired to one state. Moving it to a second is designed, not built.
  • The loop is closed for floods only. Landslide forecasts are written down but not graded. There is no live catch yet.
  • No outside users yet. No open feed, no partner intake, no sensors.
  • It runs on one PC. Two days have been missed so far.
  • Sharing data outward depends on each source's terms of use.

What is next, in order

  1. Prove it moves. The Assam soil-erosion module: a new hazard and a new state at once.
  2. Grade the landslide forecasts (they are written down now; grading needs dated landslides) and run the whole pipeline by itself, off the PC.
  3. Stamp every answer with its inputs, so any past forecast can be rebuilt.
  4. Open the feed. Only after the pipeline runs itself. A feed of stale data is worse than none.
  5. Let others write in, through a holding area, then add our own sensors.
  6. A pilot at Jang, Tawang, for ground truth in the mountains.
25 Oct

NESFIC applications close. The Assam module is our entry. Its design and plan are written. The build has not started.

Watch out for

  • Either forecast page has a one-page report button. It downloads a printable page with both forecasts for the place on screen: useful to hand over at the end.
  • A SlideSense class is a rank, not a chance. "High" means "look here first". Each level now carries a measured figure: places and days at High have had about 3 times the usual landslides, Very High about 10 times (from 84 dated landslides, so rough).
  • It is October, so the flood screens are quiet. Say it first.

Questions you will get

Short answers to the likely ones

What exactly is the Data Backbone?

A standing system that collects every useful source, keeps the originals, lines everything up on one map of the state, keeps it fresh, hands it to products, and records what they said and what really happened.

Is it a product, or plumbing?

Today it is the engine under our two products. Later it is a product in its own right, through an open feed others build on.

Why not just build the landslide app?

Because the app is the last small part. The data underneath is most of the work, and it is the same data every hazard needs. Built once, it makes each next product cheap.

The data is public. What is yours?

The assembly, the upkeep and the checked history. Twenty-nine sources made to fit one map, kept current, with every forecast graded. Anyone can download the same files. Few will do the rest.

Who else would use it?

Road and infrastructure planners, power and telecom operators, insurers, researchers and agencies, the state's own systems, other startups. None yet. The open feed is planned.

How do you add a new hazard, or a new state?

A hazard brings its own two questions and its own record. Everything else is already there. A state needs a region switch, its own local records and its own checking. Assam is the first test.

What stops Google or ISRO doing this?

They could build the pipeline. The hard parts are local: getting these sources to fit, knowing which official layer is unusable, and seasons of forecasts checked against these rivers and slopes.

Is it live?

The backbone and two products are. The loop runs for floods. The open feed, partner intake and sensors are planned.

How good are the products?

Landslide WHERE picks the right spot 6 times in 7. At a gauged river, 20% means 20%. Never one headline number.

Has it caught a real event?

Not yet. It was tested hard on past years. The next monsoon is the proof.

Not in our docs: pricing and market size. The shape we do have is the ladder. A free statewide layer, then paid tiers.

Numbers, and what not to say

Ten figures, kept short

29sources lined up, about 308 GB of raw files
8.2 millionsquares of 100 m on the shared map, 34 facts each
26 yearsof daily rain for every place, no gaps
1.9 millionriver gauge readings, some back to 1971
2products live on one backbone
2 fileswhat the first flood module added of its own
4 of 5erosion ingredients already in the backbone
4,032flood forecasts written down since 21 Sep. 1,938 graded

25 OctNESFIC application closes

Do not say

"We are a landslide app", or leading with the forecast.
Lead with the backbone. The products are the proof.
"Others already build on it", or "the feed is open".
Planned. Two of our own products stand on it today.
"It works for any state."
Designed to. Assam is the first test.
"The loop is closed."
It is, for floods. Landslides are next.
"We own unique data."
Most inputs are public. Ours is the assembly and the checked record.
"It is X% accurate", "we caught a real event", "safe", or a landslide class as a percentage.
Name the thing and its number. Not yet. Very Low. A rank.
Anything planned as if it is live: sensors, SMS alerts, the open feed.
"That is where it is going." Several of these sit on the pitch-deck slides.

One naming point

Since 11 October 2026 the whole platform is SlopeSense, the Hazard Intelligence Platform ("SHIP"), as the pitch deck has always called it. Its landslide module is SlideSense, its flood module FloodSense, and the shared pipeline under both is the Data Backbone. Before that date the landslide module was itself called SlopeSense, and the first, separate landslide app still is.

Screen guide

What every item on the two Forecast screens means

Each picture is the real screen with its items numbered. The list under it says, in a line or two, what each number is. Click a picture to enlarge it. Captured on 11 October 2026 from the app running on this PC.

SlideSense Forecast page

Open SlideSense and search a town. This is Itanagar. The numbers in the pictures are that day's; the meaning of each item does not change.

The top of the screen: the state, the place, the map · items 1 to 17

  1. 1
    Title and status. The green dot and “Live rain · 11 Oct to 17 Oct” say the rain feed is working and which seven days the forecast covers.
  2. 2
    Place search. Type a town or village to see its forecast. “My location” uses your device; “Recentre” takes the map back to the whole state.
  3. 3
    Key. The kinds of number on this screen. Outlook is the landslide level. Ground is how weak the slope is. Input is the rain. Record is past mapped landslides. “×” means times the usual number of landslides, never a chance.
  4. 4
    Land at High or above. The share of all scored land in the state that is at High or Very High on the chosen day. A share of land, not a chance.
  5. 5
    Very High. The same, for the top level alone.
  6. 6
    Most affected district. The district with the largest share of its own land at High or above that day.
  7. 7
    Road at High or above. Kilometres of main road that cross ground at High or above. The Roads page shows where.
  8. 8
    Unusually wet points. Rain is read at 219 points. This counts how many have had rain in their own wettest 10% since 2010. Zero means nowhere is unusually wet.
  9. 9
    Wettest point. The most rain at any one of those points that day.
  10. 10
    The place card. The answer for the place you searched. The word is its level, Very Low to Very High. “0.2× the usual” means places at this level have had about a fifth of the usual number of landslides. The seven bars are the next seven days.
  11. 11
    The map. Every square of ground coloured by its level for the chosen day. The pin is your place and the bright line is the state border. Grey is ground that is not scored: flat land, water, ice, or outside the state.
  12. 12
    2D / 3D. Switches between the flat map and a 3D view of the terrain. The 3D view is still being worked on.
  13. 13
    This ground. How weak this slope is, from its shape, soil, rock and land cover. No rain in it, so it is the same every day. “0.3×” means slopes like this have had about a third of the landslides of average ground.
  14. 14
    Rain today. How unusual the last 3 and 7 days of rain are for this exact spot. “0.2×” means that with rain like this, landslides have been about a fifth as common as on a usual day here.
  15. 15
    Rain that day. Millimetres of rain on the chosen day at the nearest rain point.
  16. 16
    Rain, 7 days. Total rain over the week ending that day.
  17. 17
    Map colours. The five levels. Beside each: its “times the usual” figure, and the share of land at that level.

The week, the districts and the roads · items 18 to 20

  1. 18
    7 days. One button per day with this place's figure for that day. Click a day and the whole screen moves to it. The last three are dashed because rain forecasts are weaker that far ahead.
  2. 19
    Districts to watch. Districts ranked by the share of their own land at High or above on the chosen day.
  3. 20
    Roads. Kilometres of main road crossing ground at High or above today. The button opens the Roads page, which shows the stretches.

The detail for this place · items 21 to 25

  1. 21
    Next 7 days here. One bar per day for this place: weak ground multiplied by unusual rain. Taller is worse. The line underneath names the worst day in the week.
  2. 22
    Day by day. The same week as a table: the rain in millimetres, the trigger (how unusual that rain is, from 0 to 1) and the level it gives.
  3. 23
    One-page forecast report. A printable one-page summary of this place's forecast, to hand to someone.
  4. 24
    All districts table. Opens a table with every district's figures for the day.
  5. 25
    How to read these levels. Opens the plain explanation of what a level means, how it was tested and what the forecast does not cover.

FloodSense Forecast page

Open FloodSense and search a town. This is Pasighat. It is October, so the rivers are quiet and almost every number is low.

The top of the screen: the state, the place, the map · items 1 to 18

  1. 1
    Title and issue time. “Issued 11 Oct · 10:10” is when this forecast was made. The dot is green when it is today's.
  2. 2
    Place search. Type a town or village. “My location” uses your device; “Recentre” takes the map back to the whole state.
  3. 3
    Run now. Makes a fresh forecast on the spot. It takes one to three minutes, so never press it in front of people.
  4. 4
    Key. The six kinds of number. Forecast: the chance a gauged river reaches its line, checked daily. Outlook: an approximate chance of a flood within about 10 km. Estimate: if a flood comes, the chance this spot is under water. Measured: a real gauge reading. Input: rain or soil wetness. Record: floods confirmed in the past.
  5. 5
    Flood anywhere. The chance of at least one recorded flood somewhere in Arunachal in the next seven days.
  6. 6
    Areas at 10%+. The state is split into 1,832 areas about 10 km across that have ground a flood can reach. This counts those with a 10% or higher outlook.
  7. 7
    Rivers at 10%+. Of the 32 gauged rivers, how many have a 10% or higher chance of reaching their line this week.
  8. 8
    Highest river. The gauged river with the highest chance, with its name and day.
  9. 9
    Above line now. Rivers whose latest readings are already above their line. “None” is the quiet answer.
  10. 10
    Gauges reporting. How many of the 32 gauges sent readings. Amber means a whole feed is down at its source; here the small-river feed is, so 15 gauges are offline.
  11. 11
    The place card. The answer for the place you searched: the chance of a flood within about 10 km over the next seven days, in words and as a percentage. The bars are the seven days.
  12. 12
    The map. Flood outlook for the week. Rivers with a gauge are the thick bright lines, and each gauge label shows its chance. The pin is your place.
  13. 13
    Layers. Chooses what the map shows.
  14. 14
    If a flood comes. The chance water reaches this exact spot if a flood is reported nearby. It comes from the shape of the land: height above the river, the river's size, how closed-in the valley is. The same every day.
  15. 15
    River reaches its line. The checked forecast for the gauge on this place's own river: the chance it reaches its danger line, and the highest day. This is not the same as the flood chance near here.
  16. 16
    River now. The latest daily high at that gauge, shown against its danger level. “−4.4 m” means 4.4 metres below it.
  17. 17
    Floods on record. How many flood days are confirmed within 10 km of here since 2003, by radar, a satellite flood map or a gauge.
  18. 18
    Map colours and symbols. The five chance bands, from Very low (under 2%) to High (25% and over), each with the share of land in it. Below: the symbols for a gauge, a gauged river, other rivers, and the area that drains to your place.

The week and the rivers · items 19 to 21

  1. 19
    7-day outlook. The whole week first, then one button per day, for the place you searched. Click one and the screen moves to that day. Days 4 to 7 are dashed because rain forecasts are weaker that far ahead.
  2. 20
    Rivers / Rain / Soil. Three views of what is behind the forecast: the gauged rivers, the rain, and how wet the soil is.
  3. 21
    River list. The rivers with the highest chance. Each row: the gauge, which agency runs it (CWC or NWDP), its day of highest chance, a small graph of the last 30 days against its line (dashed red), and its chance. A crossed circle means the gauge is offline.

What changed, what needs a look, and the record · items 22 to 24

  1. 22
    What changed. Today's numbers against the previous forecast: the state, your place, how many areas moved up or down a band, the rivers rising or easing most, and rivers above their line.
  2. 23
    Needs attention. Anything worth a look in today's numbers: high chances, a feed that is down, gauges offline. “Nothing stands out” is the quiet answer.
  3. 24
    Track record. The score sheet. River forecasts written down before the day, how many have since been checked against the real gauge, and how often a river truly reached its line. Below: how the level forecast is doing.

One river in detail, and every gauge · items 25 to 36

  1. 25
    Rivers panel. Pick any gauge from the list. It opens on the gauge for your place's own river.
  2. 26
    Latest daily high. The highest reading of the most recent complete day at this gauge.
  3. 27
    Its line. The level that counts as a flood here: the official danger level where one exists, otherwise the river's own wettest 2% of days.
  4. 28
    Highest chance. The highest chance this week that the river reaches its line, with the day and what it is based on (rain, the river reading, or both).
  5. 29
    Expected high. Our forecast of the river's level for the next day, with the likely range.
  6. 30
    Level graph. The last 30 days of measured daily highs (solid line), our forecast of the level (dotted, after “Now”), and the official lines across it: highest ever, danger, warning, and the river's typical level.
  7. 31
    Chance bars. Our chance, for each coming day, that the river reaches its line.
  8. 32
    Every gauge × every day. All 32 gauges down the side, the seven days across, each cell the chance in percent. A dot means well under 0.1%. Click a row to open that river's graph.
  9. 33
    One-page forecast report. A printable one-page summary of this place's flood forecast.
  10. 34
    All river gauges table. Opens the full table of every gauge with its readings and chances.
  11. 35
